extracted.intended_audience: mathematically mature self-learners (talented high-school students, math undergraduates, physics/CS majors, math PhD students) and other curious readers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and conventions for reading and using an expansive, informal but self-contained higher-mathematics textbook (Evan Chen's Napkin). Targets self-study, selective chapter reading, and pedagogical use rather than formal course replacement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisites: mathematical maturity
rubrics_metrics.description: As explained in the preface, the main prerequisite is some amount of mathematical maturity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expectation: know how to read and write a proof, follow logical arguments, and basic terminology about sets and functions (e.g. 'what is a bijection?'). If not familiar, consult Appendix E.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deciding what to read: non-linear navigation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no need to read this book in linear order: it covers many areas and there are many paths you can take.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the dependency chart (Chapter 0) to find the shortest path to a chapter you find interesting; simply pick a chapter and follow optional/required dotted arrows as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-tiered exercises hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three hierarchies: inline questions, inline exercises, and chapter-end trickier problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inline questions: offensively easy to internalize definitions. Inline exercises: more meaty but not tricky. Chapter-end problems: range from reasonable to legitimately difficult olympiad-style problems; harder problems are marked with up to three chili peppers (difficulty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem importance markings (normal / daggered / starred)
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems are marked by how important they are to the big picture: normal, daggered, and starred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normal: fun but non-central. Daggered: interesting results one should know but usually not used later. Starred: results which will be used later in the book (helps avoid hidden prerequisites).

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty annotation: chili peppers
rubrics_metrics.description: Harder problems are marked with up to three chili peppers to indicate increasing difficulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use chili-pepper count to estimate challenge level; several hints and solutions appear in Appendices B and C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical philosophy: natural explanations supersede proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: The book places a strong emphasis on explaining why a theorem should be true rather than always writing down its proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs that are mere completeness are often omitted unless there is an idea worth seeing; understanding 'why' may be via full proof, the idea of a proof, or key examples with cheerleading. The book is not intended as a replacement for dedicated courses or research training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read with pencil and paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Read this book with pencil and paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: you cannot keep everything in your head; write in margins or use a notebook to internalize definitions and computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and emphasis on examples and prototypical examples
rubrics_metrics.description: The author is pathologically obsessed with examples and places all examples in large boxes; prototypical examples are highlighted in red.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whenever a definition or theorem appears, test it against the prototypical example to see intuition and why the theorem should be true; examples are used as primary tools for understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventions: natural numbers are positive
rubrics_metrics.description: The set N is the set of positive integers, not including 0. In set theory chapters, ω = {0,1,...} is used instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of this convention when reading claims involving N versus ω.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation preference for subsets and set operations
rubrics_metrics.description: The author generally uses ⊆ and ⊊ since these are non-ambiguous, and only uses ⊂ on rare occasions where equality obviously does not hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also prefers S \ T to S − T. Power sets are denoted 2^S or P(S).

rubrics_metrics.name: Function notation conventions (f_pre, f_img, restriction, injective/surjective arrows)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f: X → Y the author uses f_pre(T) for pre-image of T and f_img(S) for image of S; f↾S denotes restriction; f : X ,→ Y denotes injective and f : X ↠ Y denotes surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abbreviate f_pre({y}) to f_pre(y); f_pre(y) is called a fiber. Note: f_img(S) is the author's preferred image notation instead of f(S).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cycle notation for permutations
rubrics_metrics.description: Permutations on finite sets may be denoted in cycle notation (e.g., (1 2 3 4)(5 6 7)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usage is context-dependent and usually obvious from examples; see Wikipedia link cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rings and algebra conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: All rings have a multiplicative identity 1 unless otherwise specified. 0 = 1 is allowed in general rings but not in integral domains. All rings are commutative unless otherwise specified. An algebra always has 1 but need not be commutative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is an elaborate naming scheme for noncommutative/graded variants used in specific chapters (e.g., graded ring, anticommutative ring). Pay attention to chapter-specific exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance and use of the Axiom of Choice
rubrics_metrics.description: The book accepts the Axiom of Choice, and uses it freely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should be aware that some theorems or arguments may implicitly rely on choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation for isomorphism and homotopy
rubrics_metrics.description: The author uses ∼= for an 'isomorphism'-style relation (an isomorphism in a reasonable category). The only time ≃ is used is for homotopic paths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be sensitive to the distinction: ∼= indicates isomorphism-like equivalence, ≃ indicates homotopy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appendices and further reading as canonical referral points
rubrics_metrics.description: Appendix A and other appendices contain pedagogical comments, references, glossary of notation, and solutions/hints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a topic or notation is unfamiliar or if you want deeper references, consult the indicated appendices and bibliography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and intent: not a course replacement
rubrics_metrics.description: This book is not intended as a replacement for dedicated books or courses; its goal is to give the reader a feeling for topics rather than emulate a full semester.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect many omitted completeness proofs and emphasis on memorable ideas; use as overview before diving into deeper texts if desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-to-chapter linkage: starred problems indicate future use
rubrics_metrics.description: Starred problems are results which will be used later in the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use star markings to identify hidden prerequisites you should learn if you want to follow later chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributing corrections and source availability
rubrics_metrics.description: The project source is hosted on GitHub (https://github.com/vEnhance/napkin) and pull-requests are welcome; corrections/comments may be emailed to evan@evanchen.cc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers are encouraged to submit errata, suggestions, and contributions; the work is described as an incomplete draft and actively maintained.
